 COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — As Ohio families face rising costs, changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) are raising concerns about access to food, particularly for people who rely on neighborhood convenience stores.
 Jayla Jemison, who previously received SNAP benefits, said the assistance helped her feed her family.
 “If it wasn't for SNAP benefits, I would not have been able to feed myself or my family,” Jemison said.
 New eligibility requirements have contributed to a decline in the number of Ohioans receiving benefits. In August 2025, nearly 1.4 million Ohioans received SNAP benefits. By August 2026, that number had fallen to just over 1.2 million, according to figures cited in the reporting. Nearly 70,000 children also lost coverage during that period.
 The changes come as food banks report continued demand for assistance.
 “They're making trade-offs between affording food or affording transportation. A majority of folks have had to make that choice. So sometimes they're turning to our food banks for help,” said Joree Novotny, Executive Director of the Ohio Association of Foodbanks.
 New restrictions raise questions for convenience stores 
 Additional SNAP restrictions are scheduled to take effect in November, including changes to which products can be purchased with benefits. Under Ohio's new rules, SNAP benefits will no longer be accepted for sugary and carbonated drinks.
 The changes have raised questions about whether some retailers will continue accepting SNAP or stop participating in the program altogether.
 A viewer contacted ABC 6 after seeing signs at the Murphy USA convenience store on Columbus' east side, stating the store would stop accepting SNAP benefits entirely beginning in November.
 During a visit to the store, ABC 6 spoke with a clerk who said the signs could be misleading. The clerk said that, to her understanding, EBT payments would still be accepted as long as the store complied with Ohio Department of Job and Family Services regulations.
 The clerk was unsure whether the signs referred to the new restrictions on certain drinks or a broader decision to stop accepting SNAP.
 For customers who rely on nearby convenience stores, losing access to SNAP at those locations could mean finding another place to shop.
 “I think that's very inconvenient because a lot of people that are on SNAP or EBT, they do not have transportation. And so therefore, the convenience store would be the most convenient place to get food and things like that,” Jemison said.
 “When a neighborhood store chooses to stop accepting SNAP, it doesn’t just make grocery shopping harder for single moms. It affects the whole community," nonprofit Motherful told ABC 6. 
 "For a mom without a car, the nearest store that takes SNAP could suddenly be a bus ride (or two) away. That extra time and stress show up everywhere: at work, at home, and in our kids’ ability to focus in school. We saw how quickly families can be pushed into crisis last November, when SNAP benefits were paused, and our community came together to raise nearly $30,000 to help moms put food on the table. Food insecurity is already a daily reality for too many moms across this country, and decisions like this land hardest on the families with the least room to absorb them. We hope Murphy USA will reconsider.”
 Food banks warn of gaps in grocery access 
 Novotny said convenience stores and smaller-format retailers play an important role in providing food access in parts of Ohio without full-service grocery stores.
 “We did some analysis of the existing 10,000 or so SNAP-authorized retailers in Ohio. And we found that more than a third of all zip codes in Ohio rely solely on C store and small format stores have no full service grocery stores,” Novotny said.
 Another federal requirement could create additional challenges for smaller retailers. Novotny said a U.S. Department of Agriculture rule expected to take effect in early November would require stores to stock a greater variety and depth of food categories.
 She said meeting those requirements could be difficult for convenience stores and other small-format retailers.
 ABC 6 sent the Ohio Department of Job and Family Services questions about the new restrictions, including what guidance the state is providing SNAP retailers, why some stores might stop accepting benefits altogether and how the changes could affect recipients.
 The department did not directly answer those questions.
 ABC 6 is awaiting a response from Murphy USA corporate.
